title: The order of the ragas
hookLine: the Granth moves from Sri Rag to Jaijavanti, thirty-one ragas in a fixed order

cards: Sri, Majh, Gauri, Asa, Gujri. Say them aloud and they almost sound like a line of poetry.
They're the first five raga sections of the Guru Granth Sahib, in order, and the list keeps going, section after section, until it reaches Jaijavanti near the end of the book.
The order is fixed; it's part of the Granth's shape. Know a hymn's raga, and you know which stretch of the book it lives in.

teach.h: SRI TO JAIJAVANTI, IN A FIXED ORDER.
teach.b: Here's the list as the Granth gives it.

Sri, Majh, Gauri, Asa, Gujri, Devgandhari, Bihagra, Vadhans, Sorath, Dhanasari, Jaitsri, Todi, Bairari, Tilang, Suhi, Bilaval, Gond, Ramkali, Nat Narayan, Mali Gaura, Maru, Tukhari, Kedara, Bhairo, Basant, Sarang, Malar, Kanara, Kalyan, Prabhati, Jaijavanti.
Sikh tradition counts thirty-one main ragas, and some sections also hold mixed forms, named in their headings, like Gauri Purbi. Notice what kind of order this is.

teach.h: ORDERED BY SOUND, NOT BY AUTHOR.
teach.b: It isn't by author: Guru Nanak doesn't get a book of his own. It isn't by date. It's by sound.
Open the Granth at a raga and you're inside one mood, and every voice there speaks in it. Inside each section there's a second order.

The Gurus' hymns come first, by Mahala, then the Bhagats: Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and others, in the same raga. So a weaver of Banaras and a Guru of the Punjab can share a page, under one heading, sung in one tune.
Why this sequence and not another? The Granth doesn't say. Scholars have suggested reasons; the text itself is silent, and it's fair to leave it there.
What the order does, plainly, is turn the book into a walk through moods: earnest, longing, hopeful, grieving, joyful, still. A reader going straight through moves from feeling to feeling.
Over the coming weeks this block walks the list a raga at a time, starting tomorrow at the beginning.

how: In a sahaj path or akhand path, a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, readers move through the raga sections in this fixed order, from Sri Rag to Jaijavanti.

games.q: what does “the order of the ragas” mean?
o: the order in which the Gurus were born
the fixed sequence of raga sections through the Granth
the sequence of hymns sung at one evening service

it's ordered by raga; every voice in a section shares its mood.
Bhagats like Kabir and Ravidas appear inside the raga sections

games.q: you're arranging a book of hymns by many voices across many years. how do you order it?
o: by raga, every voice in a section sharing one mood.
by the date each hymn was written.
games.why: the Granth is ordered by raga, so a Guru and a Bhagat can share a page, under one heading, sung in one tune.

practice: The list is on your screen: read it slowly, one name to a breath, Sri on the way in and letting it go on the way out, then Majh, then Gauri, and if a name catches you, give it a second breath.
You won't remember them all, and you don't need to; you're walking the length of the book by its moods. If you pray, let the last breath, after Jaijavanti, carry a quiet Waheguru.
